reply.title: At the Highest Point
reply.story: When you toss a ball straight up into the air, it slows down as it rises, pauses for a brief instant at its highest point, and then speeds up as it falls back down. It is tempting to think that because the ball stops moving for a split second at the top, its acceleration must also be zero at that exact moment. After all, if it is not moving, how can it be changing its speed? But let us look closer at what happens to the velocity. Just before reaching the top, the velocity is positive; just after, it is negative. The rate at which that velocity changes never stops. Gravity pulls down on the ball continuously throughout the entire flight, whether the ball is moving up, pausing at the apex, or falling back down.
reply.cardDescription: Explore what happens to velocity and acceleration when a ball is thrown straight up. See why the velocity is zero at the top while the downward acceleration remains constant at $9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
reply.instructions: Adjust the launch speed and press Play to observe how the ball moves. Use the scrubber or the At top button to examine the instant when the ball reaches its apex.
